0.title: Jesus and the Apostles: One Gospel, Two Moments
0.overview:
Read the four Gospels and then turn to the letters of Paul, and a question can quietly form in the mind of an honest reader: are these the same message? Jesus walks the roads of Galilee announcing, “The kingdom of God is at hand” (Mark 1:15). He tells parables about mustard seeds and lost sheep, heals the sick, and calls men to follow Him. Then Paul stands up and preaches, “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures … he was raised on the third day” (1 Cor. 15:3–4), and unfolds justification by faith apart from works of the law. On the surface the accent seems to fall in different places. Jesus preaches the kingdom; the apostles preach Him.

For more than a century, skeptical scholarship has driven a wedge into that gap. Adolf von Harnack argued that Jesus taught a simple religion of the fatherhood of God and the value of the soul, which the church later buried under doctrine. William Wrede went further and called the apostle Paul “the second founder of Christianity” — as if the gospel of grace and the cross were Paul’s invention, laid over the top of a simpler Jesus. In our own day the same instinct survives in a softer form: the “red-letter” impulse that prizes the words of Jesus and treats the letters of the apostles as a lesser, more complicated appendix.

This study exists to answer that wedge — not by flattening the real differences, but by locating them where they belong. There are not two gospels. There is one gospel, proclaimed at two moments in the great drama of redemption. Before the cross, Jesus announces the kingdom that is arriving; He is the King, and He speaks of His death in shadow and promise. After the cross and the empty tomb, the apostles announce the kingdom that has arrived; the King has been enthroned through His death and resurrection, and now they proclaim what He accomplished. The difference between them is the difference between “it is at hand” and “it is finished.”

So the deepest truth is more thrilling than the skeptics ever guessed. Jesus is not merely the first preacher of the gospel; He is its content. He came proclaiming the good news, and He came to be the good news. The apostles do not replace His message with their own — they preach the Christ He is. When we learn to hear the Gospels and the Epistles as one voice, the Bible opens like a single, unbroken song: the King who announced His reign, reigning now from a throne that was once a cross.

1.title: Two Gospels? — The Wedge Between Jesus and the Apostles
1.overview:
The suspicion is old and it is stubborn: that the simple prophet of Nazareth was one thing, and the church that grew up around Him was another. Jesus, it is said, preached a kingdom of love and mercy; His followers turned Him into a sacrifice and built a system of theology He never taught. Harnack’s famous lectures put it memorably — the gospel Jesus preached had to do with the Father, and not the Son. Strip away the later doctrine, he urged, and you find a religion of the heart. Wrede’s verdict on Paul was blunter still: the apostle was a second founder, and of the two founders Paul “has exercised without question the stronger … influence.”

The wedge feels plausible because the surface really does differ. Jesus rarely says in so many words, “Believe in Me and your sins will be forgiven for I will die in your place.” Paul rarely quotes Jesus’ parables. The Gospels are full of Galilee, crowds, healings, and kingdom; the Epistles are full of the cross, justification, the church, and the risen Lord. A reader who has never been shown how these fit can be forgiven for feeling the seam.

But the wedge cannot survive contact with the texts themselves. Paul insists that the gospel he preaches is not his own construction: “I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1:12). And he pronounces a double curse on anyone — himself or an angel — who would preach “a gospel contrary to the one” already received (Gal. 1:8–9). The apostle who is accused of inventing a second gospel is the very man who says there is only one, and that it came from Christ.

More decisive still, it was Jesus Himself who commissioned the apostolic message. On resurrection evening He opened the Scriptures and declared that the Christ must suffer and rise, “and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations” (Luke 24:47). The content of every apostolic sermon — a crucified and risen Savior, offered to the nations — is not a departure from Jesus. It is His own commission, carried out.
1.text:
“I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel — not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ. But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed.” (Gal. 1:6–8 ESV)

“For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.” (Gal. 1:11–12 ESV)

“Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things.” (Luke 24:46–48 ESV)

verseByVerse.quote: The gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel … I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the whole theory of Paul-the-inventor collapses at its foundation. Paul does not claim to have improved on Jesus, nor to have received a message from the earlier apostles that he then embellished. He claims the gospel came to him from Christ Himself — the same Christ who taught in Galilee now teaching Paul from glory. The line runs unbroken: the risen Jesus is the source of the apostolic gospel, so the apostolic gospel cannot be a rival to Jesus’ own. It is His voice, still speaking.

Notice the weight Paul places on origin. A gospel that were merely “man’s” could be revised, negotiated, softened to taste. But a gospel received by revelation from the Lord is fixed; it can only be guarded or betrayed. This is why Paul can pronounce a curse in the same breath (Gal. 1:8). He is not defending his ego. He is defending the one message his Master entrusted to him. (cf. 1 Cor. 15:3; Eph. 3:2–3)

verseByVerse.quote: From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse is sometimes misread, as if Paul were dismissing the earthly Jesus in favor of a heavenly idea. He is doing the opposite. Paul once “regarded Christ according to the flesh” — that is, he sized Jesus up by worldly standards and judged Him a failed, cursed pretender, and so persecuted His church. The cross and resurrection shattered that estimate. Now Paul knows the same Jesus rightly — as the crucified and risen Lord.

The point is not a different Christ but a truer sight of the one Christ. The apostles are not offering the world a philosophy detached from the Nazarene; they are offering the very Jesus who walked to Golgotha, now understood in the blazing light of Easter. The change is in the eyes that see, not in the Savior who is seen.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it is written … that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we want to know whether the apostles preached a different message than Jesus, here is the answer from Jesus’ own lips. On the evening of the resurrection He gives them their commission, and every element of the later apostolic sermons is already present: the Christ must suffer; He rises on the third day; and in His name repentance and forgiveness are to be preached to all nations. Read the sermons in Acts and you find this template filled in, city by city.

So the apostolic gospel is not an overgrowth on Jesus’ teaching. It is His teaching, unsealed. What He spoke in shadow before the cross He now sends His witnesses to proclaim in the full light of accomplished salvation. The Preacher of the kingdom is the Author of the apostles’ message. (cf. Acts 2:38; Acts 17:30–31)

1.theology:
Reformed theology has always confessed one covenant of grace administered through the whole of Scripture — the same salvation promised in Eden, pictured in Israel, accomplished at Calvary, and proclaimed to the nations. That confession is the deep reason there can be only one gospel. Because there is one God, one Mediator, and one saving purpose, the message of Jesus and the message of His apostles cannot be two competing religions. They are two stages of a single, sovereign work.

This is why the older liberalism, for all its learning, misread the evidence so badly. It assumed that doctrine is a corruption of experience — that the cross-centered theology of Paul must be a later, colder deposit over the warm ethics of Jesus. But Scripture knows nothing of a gospel without a cross. Jesus went to Jerusalem on purpose to die (Mark 10:45; Luke 9:51); the apostles simply announce what He came to do. The difference between them is not doctrine-versus-experience. It is promise-versus-fulfillment — and both belong to the one gracious plan of God.
1.examples:
Then: The wedge is not merely academic. In the second century Marcion tried to sever the God of Jesus from the God of the Old Testament and even to cut Paul loose from the other apostles, keeping only the parts that fit his scheme. The church rejected him — and in doing so confessed that the whole Bible tells one story with one Savior. Every generation faces some version of Marcion’s temptation: to keep the Jesus we like and quietly discard the rest.

Now: The modern form is gentler and therefore easier to miss. It is the believer who loves the “red letters” but skims the epistles as though Paul were an intrusion. It is the church that preaches a kind Jesus of acceptance but grows embarrassed by the cross and the call to repent. The remedy is not to love Jesus less but to trust Him more — enough to receive the very apostles He appointed, and to hear in their words the message He Himself sent them to preach.

2.title: “The Kingdom Is at Hand” — Jesus’ Own Proclamation
2.overview:
Mark sums up the whole ministry of Jesus in a single sentence of preaching: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:14–15). Every word is loaded. The time is fulfilled — the long ache of Israel’s waiting has reached its hour. The kingdom of God is at hand — God’s royal reign is breaking into history. Repent and believe — the only fitting response is a turned life and a trusting heart. And note the word Jesus uses for His own message: the gospel. Before a single apostle preaches, Jesus is already calling His announcement good news.

We must hear what “kingdom” meant on His lips. It is not first a place but a reign — the dynamic, saving rule of God. Where God reigns, demons flee, the sick are healed, sins are forgiven, and the poor hear good news. This is why Jesus can say the kingdom is “in the midst of you” (Luke 17:21): the King is standing there. The reign arrives in His person. To meet Jesus is to meet the kingdom walking.

Yet there is a veil over His preaching before the cross. Again and again He silences demons and even disciples who would announce Him too soon (Mark 8:30; Mark 9:9). This restraint — often called the “messianic secret” — is not evasion but timing. The people longed for a conquering king; Jesus would reign, but through a cross, and the meaning of His messiahship could only be safely revealed once that cross had been raised. He guards the mystery until the hour of its unveiling.

So the cross is present in Jesus’ preaching, but spoken in shadow. “The Son of Man must suffer many things” (Mark 8:31). “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24). “The Son of Man came … to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The apostles would one day preach the cross in broad daylight. Jesus preaches it at dawn — real, certain, but not yet finished. He is the King announcing a throne the world cannot yet see.
2.text:
“Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God, and saying, ‘The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.’” (Mark 1:14–15 ESV)

“And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them, ‘Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.’” (Luke 4:20–21 ESV)

“For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45 ESV)

verseByVerse.quote: The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two words carry the freight. “The time is fulfilled” translates a word for the appointed, decisive moment — not clock-time ticking by, but the hour God had marked on the calendar of redemption from before the world began. Centuries of promise now bend toward this instant. And “is at hand” renders a verb that means has come near, has drawn up close. The kingdom is not a distant rumor; it has arrived at the door in the person of the One speaking.

Then comes the response — repent and believe — and it is exactly the response the apostles will later demand (Acts 2:38; Acts 20:21). This is worth dwelling on. The very posture Jesus calls for at the start of His ministry is the posture Peter and Paul call for after the resurrection. The gospel’s summons does not change across the cross; only the fullness of what is believed. From the first sermon to the last, the door into the kingdom is a turned heart that trusts.

verseByVerse.quote: Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus reads Isaiah’s promise of good news to the poor, liberty to captives, sight to the blind — and then, with every eye upon Him, He announces that the ancient words have come true today, in your hearing. It is one of the most staggering claims ever made. The prophet’s long-awaited “year of the Lord’s favor” is not merely near; it has walked into the room and taken a seat.

This is the shape of Jesus’ whole proclamation: the promises are not just about to be kept — in Him they are being kept now. The kingdom is not a program He teaches; it is a reality He embodies. Where He is, the prophets’ hope is present tense. And that presence is grace before it is demand: good news to the poor, not a ladder for the strong. (cf. Isa. 61:1–2; Matt. 11:4–5)

verseByVerse.quote: The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here, well before Calvary, Jesus states the meaning of Calvary. Ransom is a price paid to set captives free; “for many” echoes the suffering Servant of Isaiah 53, who bears the sins of many and is numbered with the transgressors. In one sentence Jesus interprets His coming death as a substitutionary, liberating price. This is not Paul’s later theory imported backward. It is the Lord’s own explanation of why He came.

So when Paul writes that Christ “gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Tim. 2:6), he is not inventing a doctrine but echoing his Master. The theology of the cross that fills the epistles is already here in the Gospels, spoken by the One about to die. The apostles preach in the light what Jesus taught in the shadow — but it is the same cross, the same ransom, the same grace. (cf. Isa. 53:11–12; 1 Tim. 2:6)

2.theology:
Two truths must be held together, and Reformed biblical theology has labored to hold them. First, Jesus is the herald of the kingdom: He proclaims that God’s saving reign has drawn near. Second, Jesus is the content of the kingdom: the reign draws near because the King has come, and it will be established through His death and resurrection. He is both the one who announces the good news and the one whose work is the good news. To pit His preaching of the kingdom against the apostles’ preaching of the cross is to miss that the kingdom comes precisely by way of that cross.

This is the “already and not yet” that runs through the whole New Testament. In Jesus the kingdom has genuinely arrived — sins are forgiven, Satan is bound, the dead are raised. Yet its consummation waits. The veil over His messiahship before the cross is a redemptive-historical necessity, not a change of message: the King must first be enthroned by dying before His reign can be preached openly to the nations. Everything Jesus says leans toward that hour.
2.examples:
Then: The crowds wanted a king who would drive out Rome and spread a banquet of national glory. When Jesus spoke of a kingdom that comes through a cross, of a Son of Man who serves and dies, many turned away disappointed (John 6:66). The reign He announced was real, but it did not match their appetite for power — and so the veil over His messiahship also protected the truth until it could be seen rightly.

Now: We are tempted to the same edit. We prize the Jesus who heals and blesses and speaks of a better world, and grow quiet about the Jesus who says He must suffer and calls us to take up a cross. But there is no kingdom without the King, and no King without His cross. To receive His good news is to receive the whole of it — the reign that comes only through the ransom He paid.

3.title: The Hinge — Cross, Resurrection, and Pentecost
3.overview:
Why does the form of the message shift at all? Why do the Gospels sound like Galilee and the Epistles like Golgotha? The answer is not that someone changed the message. The answer is that between them stands an event — the death, resurrection, and exaltation of Jesus — and after such an event, no honest witness could preach in the same tense as before. You cannot announce as finished what has not yet happened. Before the cross, the decisive act was still future; the disciples could not yet preach “Christ died for our sins and rose again,” because He had not yet died and risen.

The resurrection is the great hinge. It does not merely reverse the crucifixion; it vindicates and enthrones the Crucified. Paul says Jesus was “declared to be the Son of God in power … by his resurrection from the dead” (Rom. 1:4). Peter says God has made the crucified Jesus “both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36). What was veiled is now unveiled: the servant who died is the reigning King. And so the message must now be preached in a new key — no longer “the kingdom is coming” but “the King has been enthroned; come to Him.”

Then comes Pentecost. Jesus had promised the Spirit who would “guide you into all the truth” and “glorify me” (John 16:13–14). The apostles did not understand the cross even as it approached; they scattered. It is the risen Christ who opens their minds to the Scriptures (Luke 24:45), and the poured-out Spirit who fills them with power and understanding. The gospel they preach is not a human reconstruction of half-remembered sayings. It is the same Lord, now interpreting His own finished work through the Spirit He sent.

So Luke 24 is the true seam of the Bible. The risen Jesus stands among His disciples, opens the Law and the Prophets and the Psalms, shows that the Christ had to suffer and rise, and commissions them to preach repentance and forgiveness in His name to all nations. Everything the apostles will say flows through this moment. The Preacher of the kingdom hands His witnesses the very words they will carry to the world.
3.text:
“Then he said to them, ‘These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.’ Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.” (Luke 24:44–45 ESV)

“Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.” (Acts 2:36 ESV)

“Concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.” (Rom. 1:3–4 ESV)

verseByVerse.quote: Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures … that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things happen here that make the apostolic gospel possible. First, the risen Christ opens their minds — the same slow-hearted disciples who had failed to grasp the necessity of the cross are given, by Him, the understanding to read the whole Old Testament as pointing to a suffering and rising Messiah. Second, He commissions the message: repentance and forgiveness, in His name, to all nations. The apostles do not compose their gospel; they receive it, already formed, from the mouth of the risen Lord.

This is the decisive rebuttal to every theory that the church invented a Christ the historical Jesus never was. The template of apostolic preaching — Scripture fulfilled, Christ crucified and risen, forgiveness offered to the nations — is dictated here by Jesus Himself. Pentecost will supply the power; Luke 24 supplies the content. (cf. Acts 2:23–24; 1 Cor. 15:3–4)

verseByVerse.quote: God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the first Christian sermon reaching its summit, and it shows exactly what the resurrection changed. Peter does not say God made Jesus divine, as though He became something He was not. He declares that God has publicly installed and vindicated the crucified Jesus as the reigning Lord and Messiah. The one Israel rejected, God has enthroned. Heaven has rendered its verdict on the cross, and the verdict is a throne.

Hear how this fits the kingdom Jesus preached. He had announced that God’s reign was at hand; now Peter announces that the King has taken His seat. The kingdom has not been abandoned for a different subject — it has been inaugurated in the enthronement of the King. The apostles preach the reign of God by preaching the Lordship of the risen Jesus. (cf. Ps. 110:1; Phil. 2:9–11)

verseByVerse.quote: Declared to be the Son of God in power … by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul opens his greatest letter by defining “the gospel of God” in terms of a person: the Son, born of David’s line, and by the resurrection openly declared to be the Son of God in power. The gospel is not first a set of ideas; it is news about Jesus — His identity, His death, His vindication. And its center is the resurrection, the event that flooded the disciples’ backward glance with light and turned frightened deserters into fearless witnesses.

Set this beside Mark 1:1 — “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” — and the unity is plain. Mark calls the story of Jesus the gospel; Paul calls the risen Jesus the gospel. The apostle and the evangelist are announcing the same Christ, one before the resurrection has been proclaimed and one after. (cf. Mark 1:1; Acts 13:32–33)

3.theology:
The shift from Gospels to Epistles is a shift of redemptive-historical location, not of gospel. This is the great insight of Reformed biblical theology: revelation unfolds through the events it describes, so the message about those events necessarily deepens as they occur. Before the cross the accent falls on the King who has come and the reign that is dawning; after the resurrection the accent falls on the finished work and the enthroned Lord. Same Christ, same grace, same kingdom — now proclaimed from the far side of the empty tomb.

This also guards us from a subtle error. The apostles are not free authors improving on Jesus; they are His authorized witnesses, taught by the risen Christ and carried by His Spirit. Their word is His word (Luke 10:16; John 16:13–14). To receive the apostolic gospel, therefore, is not to leave Jesus behind for His followers — it is to keep listening to Jesus, now speaking through the men He commissioned and the Spirit He poured out.
3.examples:
Then: On the road to Emmaus two disciples walked in despair, saying, “we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21) — past tense, hope buried. Then the risen Christ opened the Scriptures to them, and their hearts burned within them. Everything they would later believe and preach hung on that turning: not a new idea, but the same Jesus, alive, teaching them how to read the story they had lived through.

Now: We live entirely on the far side of the hinge. We have never known the message in its pre-Easter form; we receive it as the apostles preached it, from an empty tomb. That is a mercy. It means we are not left to piece together a religion from scattered sayings, but are handed the finished gospel by eyewitnesses whom the risen Lord Himself taught. When we read Paul, we are not straying from Jesus. We are hearing Jesus’ own commission carried out.

4.title: The Apostolic Kerygma — “Christ Died for Our Sins”
4.overview:
When we ask what the apostles actually preached, we are not left to guess. Paul preserves the earliest Christian creed, older than any of his letters, handed to him and now handed to us: “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, … he was buried, … he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and … he appeared” (1 Cor. 15:3–5). This is the irreducible core — death, burial, resurrection, appearances — and Paul calls it “of first importance.” It is what he received, not what he devised.

The sermons in Acts show the same pattern preached city by city. Whether Peter at Pentecost or Paul in the synagogue at Antioch, the shape recurs: the age of promise has been fulfilled; Jesus lived, taught, and did mighty works; He was crucified according to God’s definite plan; God raised Him and exalted Him; therefore repent, believe, and receive forgiveness. Scholars have long noticed this common outline — the apostolic kerygma, the “thing preached.” It is remarkably stable, which is why it reads like a single gospel spoken in many voices.

Out of this core the great doctrines of the epistles unfold. Justification by faith is not an alien addition; it is the courtroom meaning of “Christ died for our sins.” If He bore our sins and rose, then the verdict over the believing sinner is acquitted — “justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 3:24). Paul is not building a new religion beside Jesus. He is drawing out what it means that the King died in our place and lives to reign.

And here is the detail that quietly dismantles the whole “Jesus preached the kingdom, the church preached Christ” slogan: the apostles never stopped preaching the kingdom. Philip preaches “the kingdom of God” (Acts 8:12); Paul reasons about it in Ephesus for months (Acts 19:8); the book of Acts closes with Paul in Rome “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 28:31). The kingdom did not disappear from apostolic preaching. It arrived — in the enthroned King they proclaimed.
4.text:
“For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.” (1 Cor. 15:3–5 ESV)

“This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it.” (Acts 2:23–24 ESV)

“He lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.” (Acts 28:30–31 ESV)

verseByVerse.quote: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures … he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the oldest fragment of Christian confession we possess — a creed already fixed and “handed over” before Paul ever wrote a letter, likely within a few years of the resurrection itself. That fact alone answers the charge that the cross-centered gospel was a late invention. Long before there was a New Testament, the church was confessing that Christ died for our sins and rose on the third day, and both according to the Scriptures.

Weigh the phrase “for our sins.” The death is not a tragedy to be explained away but a substitution to be received: He died in the place of guilty people, bearing what they deserved. And “according to the Scriptures” ties it back to Isaiah’s Servant and the whole Old Testament hope — the very Scriptures Jesus opened to His disciples in Luke 24. The apostles are preaching the meaning of the cross that Jesus Himself had taught. (cf. Isa. 53:5–6; Luke 24:26–27)

verseByVerse.quote: This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God … God raised him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter holds two truths in one sentence without flinching, and the gospel lives in their union. The cross was the darkest crime in history — “you crucified and killed [him] by the hands of lawless men” — and it was the deliberate plan of God, “the definite plan and foreknowledge” settled before the world began. Human guilt is real and God’s sovereignty is total, and both meet at Golgotha. The murder of the Son was, at the same moment, the mercy of the Father.

This is the theology of the cross Jesus had spoken in shadow — “the Son of Man must suffer” (Mark 8:31) — now preached in full daylight. The “must” of the Gospels becomes the “definite plan” of Acts. The apostles are not adding to Jesus; they are announcing that what He said had to happen has happened, exactly as God intended. (cf. Mark 8:31; Acts 4:27–28)

verseByVerse.quote: Proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke ends his two-volume history with a phrase that quietly refutes a whole school of thought. Paul in Rome is doing two things that are really one: “proclaiming the kingdom of God” and “teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ.” The kingdom Jesus announced and the Christ the apostles preach are not two subjects but one — for the kingdom is the reign of God now inaugurated in the enthroned Jesus. To preach Christ as Lord is to preach the kingdom come.

So the slogan fails: it is simply not true that the apostles dropped the kingdom for the cross. From Philip in Samaria (Acts 8:12) to Paul in Rome, the kingdom remains on their lips from the first chapter of Acts to the last. What changed is that the King has been crowned. The apostles preach the kingdom precisely by preaching its King. (cf. Acts 8:12; Acts 19:8; Acts 20:25)

4.theology:
The kerygma — the fixed core of apostolic preaching — is essentially the commission of Luke 24 filled out in history. Christ crucified for sins, raised and exalted, offered to the nations for repentance and forgiveness: this is what the apostles received from the risen Lord and what they everywhere proclaimed. The doctrines the epistles develop — justification, reconciliation, redemption, adoption — are not additions to this core but its unfolding. Justification by faith is “Christ died for our sins” stated in the language of the courtroom; it is the cross applied to the guilty conscience.

Reformed theology insists, therefore, that Paul and Jesus preach one sola gratia. Jesus welcomed sinners and pronounced their sins forgiven by His sheer authority (Mark 2:5; Luke 7:48); Paul explains that this forgiveness rests on the cross and is received by faith alone. The tax collector went home justified in Luke’s Gospel (Luke 18:14) before Paul ever expounded justification in Romans. The grace is identical. The apostles simply show us its ground and its glory.
4.examples:
Then: Stand in the crowd at Pentecost. Peter preaches Jesus crucified and risen and enthroned, and the hearers are “cut to the heart” and cry, “Brothers, what shall we do?” (Acts 2:37). His answer — “Repent … and be baptized … for the forgiveness of your sins” — is the very summons Jesus began with in Galilee: repent, and receive the kingdom. Three thousand were added that day. The apostolic gospel was not a colder religion than Jesus’; it was fire.

Now: A gospel that stops at Jesus the teacher, without His death for our sins and His resurrection, has no answer for the cry “what shall we do?” It can inspire, but it cannot forgive. The apostolic message meets the guilty exactly where they are — with a crucified Savior who bore their sins and a risen Lord who reigns — and it is still the only word that can cut a heart to the quick and then heal it.

5.title: One Gospel, Two Moments — The Deep Unity
5.overview:
Now we can name plainly what unites Jesus and the apostles. It is not that their messages merely overlap. It is that they preach one gospel located at two moments on the single timeline of redemption — the difference between “the kingdom is at hand” and “it is finished.” Jesus announces the reign of God arriving in Himself and moving toward its climax at the cross; the apostles announce that the climax has come, the King is enthroned, and salvation is now accomplished and offered to the world. Promise and fulfillment — but one promise, one fulfillment, one Christ.

Several threads run unbroken across the seam. The response is the same: Jesus calls for repentance and faith (Mark 1:15), and so do the apostles (Acts 20:21). The grace is the same: Jesus gives the kingdom to the poor in spirit and the desperate tax collector, not the self-assured; Paul declares salvation “by grace … through faith … not a result of works” (Eph. 2:8–9). Neither Testament of preaching leaves room for a boast. The Christ is the same: Jesus is the content of His own message and of theirs — He came preaching the good news and He came to be it.

Above all, the Scriptures are the same. Jesus reads Isaiah and says, “Today this is fulfilled” (Luke 4:21); Paul preaches Christ “in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3). Both are opening the same Old Testament and finding the same Messiah. There is no daylight between the Bible Jesus preached from and the Bible the apostles preached from, because both are pointing to Him.

Here, then, is the wonder that answers the skeptic’s wedge. Jesus is the herald who is also the message. In the Gospels He proclaims the gospel; in the Epistles He is the gospel proclaimed. The reign He announced comes by the cross He died and the throne He now fills. To read the whole New Testament this way is to hear one voice from Galilee to Rome — the King who preached His kingdom, and then established it by dying and rising, and now calls the nations to Himself.
5.text:
“And he answered them, ‘Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.’” (Luke 7:22–23 ESV)

“I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 18:14 ESV)

“But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God. And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again.” (Acts 20:24–25 ESV)

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Long before Paul writes a word about justification, Jesus does the thing justification describes: He forgives sins, directly, by His own authority. The scribes are scandalized — “who can forgive sins but God alone?” — and they are right about the premise and wrong about the man. The One standing before them is God with them, and He dispenses pardon as freely as He heals a body. The grace the apostles will explain is already flowing here from Jesus’ own hand.

This is why the “Jesus versus Paul” contrast breaks down at the level of the actual texts. What Paul calls being “justified” — the guilty declared forgiven — Jesus simply pronounces over a paralyzed man let down through a roof. Paul gives us the ground (the cross) and the means (faith); Jesus gives us the reality, in person. Same forgiveness, same grace, one Savior. (cf. Luke 7:48–50; Rom. 3:23–24)

verseByVerse.quote: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ … this man went down to his house justified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word Paul made famous appears here on the lips of Jesus. A tax collector, unable even to lift his eyes, beats his breast and pleads for mercy — and Jesus says he went home “justified,” the very verb Romans and Galatians will unfold. Not the confident religious man with his résumé of works, but the empty-handed sinner who casts himself on mercy, is the one declared right with God. The doctrine of justification by faith is not Paul’s invention; it is Jesus’ parable.

And notice the plea itself — “be merciful to me” carries the sense “let atonement be made for me,” the language of the mercy seat where blood was sprinkled for sin. The tax collector is asking, without knowing all it would mean, for exactly what the cross would provide. Jesus grants it. The gospel of grace is one gospel, and it was already being preached — and enacted — in Galilee. (cf. Rom. 4:5; Eph. 2:8–9)

verseByVerse.quote: The gospel of the grace of God … proclaiming the kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a single farewell speech Paul lays two phrases side by side and treats them as one ministry. He has labored to testify to “the gospel of the grace of God,” and he describes that same labor as “proclaiming the kingdom.” For Paul these are not two subjects but one — the reign of God and the grace of God meet in the crucified and risen King. To preach grace is to preach the kingdom; to preach the kingdom is to preach the King who saves by grace.

This is the death of the old slogan. If the apostle to the Gentiles can call his life’s work both “the gospel of grace” and “proclaiming the kingdom” in the same breath, then Jesus’ kingdom-preaching and Paul’s grace-preaching were never rivals. They were always one gospel — the good news that God reigns to save sinners through His Son. (cf. Acts 28:31; Col. 1:13–14)

5.theology:
The unity of the two moments rests on the unity of the Christ. Reformed theology has long taught that the kingdom of God and the cross of Christ are not competing centers but one reality seen from two angles: the King reigns from the tree. Calvary is not the interruption of the kingdom program but its throne room. When Jesus is lifted up on the cross, He is enthroned; when He rises, He is vindicated; when He ascends, He takes His seat at the right hand. The reign He announced in Galilee is established by the death and resurrection the apostles proclaim.

This is why the Scriptures can speak of Jesus as both the object and the author of faith, both the preacher of the gospel and the gospel preached. He does not stand outside His message pointing to it; He is its heart. To divide His kingdom-preaching from the apostles’ Christ-preaching is finally to divide Jesus from Himself — to keep the herald and lose the message, or keep the message and silence the herald. The whole New Testament refuses the division. One Christ, one gospel, from first sermon to last.
5.examples:
Then: John the Baptist, languishing in prison, sent to ask whether Jesus really was the Coming One. Jesus’ answer was not a new doctrine but Isaiah come to life: the blind see, the lame walk, “the poor have good news preached to them” (Luke 7:22). That was the kingdom — and it was pure grace to the helpless. The same grace that raised a dead girl and cleansed a leper is the grace the apostles preach when they say Christ died for the ungodly. One kindness, one Savior, one gospel.

Now: When we read the tax collector’s prayer and then read Romans, we should feel the seam vanish. The sinner who beats his breast and the sinner Paul says is “justified by faith” are the same person receiving the same mercy. This is deeply freeing: we do not have to choose between the Jesus of the Gospels and the gospel of the apostles. To fall at Jesus’ feet crying “be merciful to me” is the gospel of grace — preached by the King and explained by His witnesses.

6.title: Guarding the One Gospel Today
6.overview:
If Jesus and the apostles preach one gospel at two moments, then two errors lie waiting on either side of the road, and both are alive in the church today. Understanding the unity is not merely an academic settlement; it is a guardrail for the soul and for the pulpit.

The first error keeps Jesus and loses the cross. It prizes the “red letters,” the teacher of love and justice and the beautiful ideals of the kingdom, but grows embarrassed by substitutionary death, by wrath and atonement, by the call to repent. This is Harnack’s ghost in modern dress — a Jesus of ethics without the Savior who bled. But a kingdom with no cross has no doorway; a Christ who only instructs cannot forgive. Strip the atonement out of Jesus and you are left with a moral example who condemns you by His very perfection and cannot save you at all.

The second error keeps the cross and loses the kingdom. It reduces the gospel to a private transaction — my sins forgiven, my ticket to heaven — and never bows before the crucified King as Lord of every acre of life. But the apostles never preached a cross without a crown. The same Paul who preached Christ crucified preached the kingdom of God to his dying day (Acts 28:31), and told the Colossians that God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins” (Col. 1:13–14) — kingdom and forgiveness fused in a single breath.

The whole-Bible gospel holds both, because Jesus and the apostles held both. The crucified and risen King forgives sins and claims the cosmos. He saves the individual sinner and reigns over all things. To guard this gospel is to keep reading the Gospels and the Epistles together — to hear Jesus and His apostles as one voice, and to bow before the one Lord they both proclaim.
6.text:
“He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent. For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile to himself all things … making peace by the blood of his cross.” (Col. 1:18–20 ESV)

“For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.” (2 Cor. 4:5 ESV)

“And Jesus came and said to them, ‘All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations … teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.’” (Matt. 28:18–20 ESV)

verseByVerse.quote: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Great Commission is the two moments joined in one scene. The crucified and risen Jesus now claims “all authority in heaven and on earth” — this is the enthroned King, the kingdom come in power. And from that throne He sends His apostles to make disciples, to baptize, to teach obedience to all He commanded. Kingdom and cross and mission stand together: the reign He announced, established by His death and resurrection, now goes to the nations through the witnesses He commissions.

Here Jesus does with His own mouth what this whole study has traced. He is the King with all authority; He sends the apostolic message; and He promises His abiding presence to the end of the age. The gospel the apostles preach is Jesus’ gospel, carried under Jesus’ authority, empowered by Jesus’ presence. There is no seam between the Christ who commands and the church that obeys. (cf. Dan. 7:14; Acts 1:8)

verseByVerse.quote: Transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In one sentence Paul fuses the two things some would tear apart. To be saved is to be “transferred … to the kingdom” — the language of Jesus’ Galilean preaching — and in the same clause it is to have “redemption, the forgiveness of sins” — the language of the cross. Kingdom and forgiveness are not two gospels laid side by side; they are one salvation described from two angles. You do not enter the kingdom apart from the forgiveness the cross secures, and you are not forgiven except into the reign of the beloved Son.

This is the answer to both modern errors at once. Against the cross-less kingdom: entry comes only through redemption in Christ’s blood. Against the kingdom-less cross: forgiveness lands us under a King, in His realm, owing Him everything. Paul will not let us have one without the other, because Christ is one. (cf. Acts 26:18; Eph. 1:7)

verseByVerse.quote: You were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God … and they shall reign on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Bible’s final vision gathers every thread of this study into one song. The One at the center of heaven’s worship is a Lamb, standing, as though it had been slain — the cross and the throne in a single image. He is worshiped because He was slain and by His blood ransomed a people (the language of Mark 10:45 come to full glory), and because that ransomed people will reign with Him (the kingdom consummated). Cross and kingdom, redemption and reign, are here forever one.

This is where Jesus’ preaching and the apostles’ preaching were always heading: the Lamb who was slain, enthroned and adored, His ransomed kingdom gathered from every tribe and tongue. The King announced His reign; He established it by His blood; and He will complete it in glory. One gospel, from the first word in Galilee to the last hallelujah of heaven. (cf. Mark 10:45; Phil. 2:9–11)

6.theology:
To guard the unity of Jesus’ and the apostles’ gospel is to guard the gospel itself, and Scripture calls this a sacred trust: “guard the good deposit entrusted to you” (2 Tim. 1:14). The deposit is one — a crucified, risen, reigning Christ who saves sinners by grace and rules the world as Lord. Every heresy that has troubled the church has, in some way, torn apart what Jesus and His apostles held together: severing law from grace, or grace from lordship, or the Jesus of history from the Christ of faith. Faithfulness means keeping the seam sealed.

And so this study ends not in the study but on the knees. If Jesus is the herald who is also the message, then the right response to both His preaching and His apostles’ is the same the tax collector gave, the same Pentecost drew, the same the Great Commission commands: repent, believe, and follow the crucified and risen King. There is one gospel, one Christ, one grace — and He bids us come. To Him, with the whole redeemed church, be glory and dominion forever. Soli Deo Gloria.
6.examples:
Then: When Paul handed the gospel to Timothy, he did not hand him a private religion or a bare kingdom-ethic. He charged him to “guard the good deposit” and to preach “Christ Jesus, who … was raised from the dead” and will “judge the living and the dead … and his kingdom” (2 Tim. 4:1). Cross and kingdom, in one charge, passed from the apostle to the next generation — exactly as it had come from Christ to the apostle.

Now: The deposit is in our hands. We are tempted, still, to keep the half of Christ we prefer — a gentle teacher without a cross, or a personal Savior without a throne. The gospel of Jesus and His apostles will not be halved. It offers a crucified King who forgives our sins and reigns over our lives and will fill the earth with His glory. To believe it whole, to preach it whole, to bow to Him whole — this is to hold the one gospel they died to deliver.
